questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Cardiac Anatomy & Circulation
questions.hintContent: Recall which coronary artery feeds the main pumping wall of the left ventricle and which artery feeds the SA and AV nodes in most people.
questions.hintStrategy: Link the vessel to the territory it perfuses, then to the complication that territory produces. Eliminate options tied to a different artery.
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client is admitted to the cardiac unit after an MI caused by a 95% occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. Current vital signs are BP 104/66, P 98, RR 20, SpO₂ 95% on room air. Based on the vessel involved, which complication should the nurse monitor for most closely?
options: New crackles, S3, and falling BP indicating left ventricular pump failure
Sudden bradycardia and heart block from sinoatrial and AV node ischemia
Jugular venous distention with clear lungs from right ventricular infarction
Unilateral leg swelling from venous stasis during bed rest
optionRationales: Correct. The LAD supplies the anterior LV wall, the anterior two-thirds of the septum, and the apex — the main pumping muscle — so an LAD occlusion places the client at high risk for left ventricular failure and cardiogenic shock.
The SA and AV nodes are supplied mainly by the right coronary artery; bradycardia and heart block are classically linked to inferior (RCA) MIs.
Right ventricular infarction (JVD with clear lungs, hypotension) is associated with RCA occlusion.
DVT is a general risk of immobility, but it is not the complication most directly linked to the vessel involved.
questions.rationale: The left main coronary artery divides into the LAD and circumflex. The LAD perfuses the anterior LV and septum, the main pumping muscle. Blockage can cause a large anterior MI with a high risk of heart failure and cardiogenic shock, so the nurse watches closely for crackles, an S3, hypotension, and falling urine output. Inferior (RCA) MIs are the ones associated with bradycardia, heart blocks, and RV infarction.
questions.takeaway: LAD = anterior LV + septum ('widow-maker'); RCA = inferior wall and the SA/AV nodes.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Sounds & Cardiac Auscultation
questions.hintContent: Think about where the apex of the heart (the point of maximal impulse) sits on the chest wall.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the mnemonic APE To Man and move from the base of the heart toward the apex.
questions.stem: A client with heart failure has gained 2 kg (4.4 lb) in 3 days. The nurse wants to auscultate the mitral area with the bell to listen for an S3. Where should the nurse place the stethoscope?
options: 2nd intercostal space, right sternal border
5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line
3rd intercostal space, left sternal border
2nd intercostal space, left sternal border
optionRationales: This is the aortic area, where S2 is loudest.
Correct. The mitral area is at the apex (PMI), 5th ICS left midclavicular line, where S1 is loudest and S3/S4 are best heard.
This is Erb's point, where both S1 and S2 can be heard.
This is the pulmonic area, where physiologic splitting of S2 is best heard.
questions.rationale: Use 'APE To Man': Aortic (2nd ICS RSB), Pulmonic (2nd ICS LSB), Erb's (3rd ICS LSB), Tricuspid (4th–5th ICS LLSB), Mitral (5th ICS left MCL). The mitral area corresponds to the apex of the heart.
questions.takeaway: Mitral = apex = 5th ICS, left midclavicular line.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Sounds & Cardiac Auscultation
questions.hintContent: Recall which extra heart sound comes after S2 and which comes before S1, and what each says about the ventricle.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the cadence in the stem ('Ken-tuc-ky') as your cue to the timing, then match timing to mechanism.
questions.stem: A 68-year-old client with heart failure is being assessed. With the bell at the apex, the nurse hears a low-pitched sound immediately after S2 that creates a 'Ken-tuc-ky' cadence. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: Normal physiologic splitting of the second heart sound
Atrial contraction against a stiff, noncompliant ventricle
Rapid ventricular filling into a volume-overloaded ventricle
Friction between inflamed pericardial layers
optionRationales: A physiologic split S2 is heard at the pulmonic area during inspiration and is two components of S2, not a separate low-pitched sound.
This describes S4, which occurs just before S1 ('Ten-nes-see').
Correct. An S3 (ventricular gallop) in early diastole reflects rapid filling into a volume-overloaded ventricle — a classic sign of heart failure in adults.
A pericardial friction rub is a scratchy, leathery sound, not a gallop.
questions.rationale: S3 follows S2 in early diastole. In children, young adults, and late pregnancy it can be normal, but in an older adult with HF it signals fluid overload and should prompt assessment of lung sounds, weight, and I&O.
questions.takeaway: S3 after S2 = volume overload ('sloshing-in'); S4 before S1 = stiff ventricle.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Lifespan Considerations
questions.hintContent: Consider what happens to blood volume and cardiac output in the third trimester and which populations may normally have an S3.
questions.hintStrategy: Look at ALL the data — vital signs, lungs, symptoms — before deciding whether a finding is pathologic. Avoid over-reacting.
questions.stem: A healthy 26-year-old client at 35 weeks' gestation has an S3 heart sound on auscultation. Vital signs are BP 112/68, P 92, RR 18, SpO₂ 99%. Lungs are clear. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Notify the provider immediately of a possible peripartum cardiomyopathy
Place the client on bed rest and restrict oral fluids
Obtain a prescription for a stat echocardiogram
Document the finding as expected for this stage of pregnancy
optionRationales: With normal vital signs, clear lungs, and no symptoms, there is no evidence of cardiomyopathy; urgent notification is not warranted.
Bed rest and fluid restriction are not indicated for an expected finding and could promote dehydration and venous stasis.
An echocardiogram is not needed for an isolated, expected finding in an asymptomatic pregnant client.
Correct. Blood volume and cardiac output increase markedly in pregnancy, and an S3 in the third trimester is a normal finding.
questions.rationale: An S3 can be normal in children, young adults, and third-trimester pregnancy because of increased ventricular filling. The nurse evaluates the whole picture — vitals, lungs, symptoms — before deciding a sound is pathologic.
questions.takeaway: Third-trimester S3 with normal findings = expected; document it.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload & Contractility
questions.hintContent: Recall the difference between preload, afterload, and contractility, and which one arterial tone controls.
questions.hintStrategy: The drug class name (arterial vasodilator) tells you which determinant it changes. Pick the explanation that matches that mechanism in lay terms.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with hypertension and heart failure is started on an arterial vasodilator. The client asks how this medication will help the heart. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: It lowers the resistance your heart has to pump against, so the heart works less.
It increases the amount of blood returning to your heart so it fills more completely.
It makes your heart muscle squeeze more forcefully with each beat.
It speeds up your heart rate so more blood is pumped every minute.
optionRationales: Correct. Arterial vasodilators reduce systemic vascular resistance (afterload), decreasing myocardial workload and oxygen demand.
Increasing venous return increases preload, which would worsen congestion in heart failure.
Increasing contractility describes a positive inotrope such as dobutamine or digoxin.
Increasing heart rate raises oxygen demand and shortens filling time; it is not the goal of vasodilator therapy.
questions.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood, driven by vascular tone. When afterload is high, myocardial oxygen consumption rises — a vicious cycle in a failing heart. Reducing afterload improves forward flow and decreases workload.
questions.takeaway: Arterial vasodilators ↓ afterload → ↓ cardiac workload.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload & Contractility
questions.hintContent: Recall the formula CO = HR × SV and when during the cardiac cycle the ventricles fill.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask yourself why a HIGHER heart rate could produce a LOWER BP — which variable in the CO formula must have fallen?
questions.stem: A client with atrial fibrillation develops a ventricular rate of 156/min. BP has fallen from 128/76 to 88/54, and the client reports lightheadedness. Which explanation best accounts for the drop in blood pressure?
options: The rapid rate increases afterload, preventing ventricular ejection.
The shortened diastole reduces ventricular filling, lowering stroke volume.
The rapid rate causes excessive preload that overstretches the myocardium.
Vagal stimulation from the rapid rate causes peripheral vasodilation.
optionRationales: Afterload is determined by vascular resistance, not by heart rate.
Correct. Very fast rates shorten diastole, so the ventricles do not fill; stroke volume falls enough that CO (HR × SV) drops despite the higher rate. Loss of the atrial kick worsens this.
Rapid rates decrease, not increase, ventricular filling (preload).
Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation slows the heart; it is not caused by tachycardia.
questions.rationale: CO = HR × SV. Increasing HR raises CO only up to a point; at rates of roughly 150 and above, filling time is so short that SV plummets. In atrial fibrillation the loss of coordinated atrial contraction further reduces filling. Coronary perfusion (which occurs in diastole) also falls.
questions.takeaway: Very fast heart rates reduce filling time → ↓ SV → ↓ CO and BP.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Conduction System & Action Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall what the PR interval and QRS duration each represent on the ECG.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each value to its normal range; the abnormal interval points to the structure involved.
questions.stem: A 79-year-old client taking a beta-blocker has a heart rate of 58/min. The rhythm strip shows a P wave before every QRS complex, a PR interval of 0.28 seconds (previously 0.18 seconds), and a QRS of 0.08 seconds. The nurse recognizes that the prolonged conduction is occurring in which structure?
options: Sinoatrial node
Purkinje fibers
Atrioventricular node
Right bundle branch
optionRationales: The SA node initiates the impulse; a P wave before every QRS shows it is firing, and its function is reflected in the rate, not the PR interval.
Purkinje fibers conduct through the ventricles; a delay there would widen the QRS, which is normal at 0.08 s.

Correct. The PR interval reflects conduction from the atria through the AV node. A PR >0.20 s indicates delayed AV nodal conduction (first-degree AV block), which beta-blockers and age-related AV node fibrosis can cause.
A bundle branch block widens the QRS (≥0.12 s); this QRS is normal.
questions.rationale: The normal pathway is SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers. The AV node normally delays the impulse so the ventricles can fill, and the PR interval (0.12–0.20 s) measures that delay. A prolonged PR with a normal QRS points to the AV node. Beta-blockers and fibrosis of the conduction system in older adults are common causes.
questions.takeaway: Long PR interval = slowed AV node conduction; wide QRS = ventricular/bundle branch problem.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure Assessment
questions.hintContent: Recall the ideal bladder size relative to arm circumference and how an undersized cuff affects the reading.
questions.hintStrategy: The reading is inconsistent with the baseline. Before acting on a number, ask whether the number is trustworthy.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with an arm circumference of 42 cm has a BP of 168/96 measured with a standard adult cuff. The client has no history of hypertension, and previous readings were 124/78 to 130/80. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the provider of new-onset stage 2 hypertension
Recheck the BP in the same arm immediately using the same cuff
Ask the client about headache, blurred vision, and chest pain
Remeasure the BP using a large adult cuff after a brief rest
optionRationales: The reading is probably inaccurate; notifying the provider before verifying it could lead to unnecessary treatment.
Repeating immediately on the same arm with the same undersized cuff reproduces the error and causes venous congestion.
Symptom assessment is reasonable, but the reading itself is unreliable and should be corrected first.
Correct. A cuff that is too small for the arm produces a falsely high reading. The bladder should encircle about 80% of the arm.
questions.rationale: Miscuffing is one of the most common BP errors; an undersized cuff can raise readings by up to 20 mm Hg. When a reading is unexpected and inconsistent with the client's baseline, the nurse first verifies it with correct technique and equipment.
questions.takeaway: Cuff too small → falsely high. Verify before you act.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure Assessment
questions.hintContent: Review the conditions that make a limb unsafe for BP measurement and how long the risk after lymph node removal lasts.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each arm against the contraindications first; if both are ruled out, consider what alternate site remains.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A client had a left mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection 2 years ago and now has an IV infusing into the right forearm. Which site is most appropriate for the nurse to measure the client's blood pressure?
options: Popliteal artery using a thigh cuff
Left brachial artery, because the surgery was 2 years ago
Right brachial artery with the IV temporarily paused
Left radial artery using a wrist cuff
optionRationales: Correct. Both arms have contraindications, so the thigh (popliteal artery) with an appropriately sized thigh cuff is the alternative site.
The risk of lymphedema after axillary node removal is lifelong; avoid BP cuffs on that arm regardless of time since surgery.
Inflating a cuff over an infusing IV can damage the vein, interrupt the infusion, and cause infiltration; pausing the IV does not remove these risks.
Any compression on the arm on the side of node dissection should be avoided, including a wrist cuff.
questions.rationale: BP should not be measured on a limb with an IV infusion, AV fistula, cast or injury, or on the side of breast/axillary surgery with lymph node removal. The thigh is the alternative; expect thigh SBP to be somewhat higher than the arm.
questions.takeaway: Both arms off-limits → use the thigh with a thigh-sized cuff.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure Assessment
questions.hintContent: Recall what an auscultatory gap is and which clients are prone to it.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask which option guarantees the cuff starts ABOVE the true systolic pressure.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with long-standing hypertension is having BP measured by auscultation. Which action by the nurse best prevents recording an inaccurate reading caused by an auscultatory gap?
options: Deflate the cuff at 5–6 mm Hg per second to shorten the measurement
Palpate the brachial pulse while inflating and then inflate 30 mm Hg above where it disappears
Record the point at which sounds become muffled as the systolic pressure
Inflate the cuff to 140 mm Hg for every client, then deflate slowly
optionRationales: Deflating too quickly causes underestimation of SBP and overestimation of DBP.
Correct. Estimating SBP by palpation ensures the cuff is inflated above the true systolic pressure so the first Korotkoff sound is not missed in the gap.
Muffling is phase IV and relates to diastolic pressure in some clients, not systolic.
A fixed inflation point may be below the true SBP of a hypertensive client, and the gap may be mistaken for the systolic value.
questions.rationale: An auscultatory gap is a temporary disappearance of Korotkoff sounds after phase I, common in hypertension and arterial stiffness. If the cuff is inflated only into the gap, the nurse records a falsely low SBP. The palpatory estimate prevents this.
questions.takeaway: Palpate first, then inflate 30 mm Hg above the point the pulse disappears.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure Assessment
questions.hintContent: Recall which Korotkoff phase marks systolic pressure and which marks diastolic pressure in adults.
questions.hintStrategy: Note that the client is an adult and a clear phase of silence was heard.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: While measuring an adult client's blood pressure, the nurse hears the first clear tapping sound at 134 mm Hg, muffling at 86 mm Hg, and silence at 80 mm Hg. How should the nurse record this BP?
options: 134/86/80 without further interpretation
optionRationales: Muffling (phase IV) is used as the diastolic value for children, not for adults with a clear phase V.
Neither value is the systolic pressure; the first clear tapping sound is systolic.
Correct. Phase I (first clear tapping) = SBP; phase V (disappearance) = DBP in adults.
A three-number recording is sometimes used when sounds persist, but here a clear phase V was heard; the standard adult recording is SBP/phase V.
questions.rationale: Korotkoff phase I marks systolic pressure. In adults, phase V (silence) is the diastolic pressure. Phase IV (muffling) is recorded as diastolic in children or when sounds continue to near zero.
questions.takeaway: Adult BP = phase I / phase V.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure Assessment
questions.hintContent: Recall the numeric criteria for orthostatic hypotension and the time frame for measurement.
questions.hintStrategy: Do the math: calculate the change in SBP, DBP, and pulse, then compare to the criteria.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client receiving furosemide reports dizziness when getting out of bed. The nurse obtains these vital signs: supine BP 128/78, P 76; standing at 3 minutes BP 104/70, P 98. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The findings are within normal limits for a position change.
Only the pulse change is significant; the BP drop is expected.
The findings cannot be interpreted without a sitting reading.
The findings meet criteria for orthostatic hypotension.
optionRationales: A 24 mm Hg SBP drop with symptoms is not a normal response to standing.
The SBP drop of 24 mm Hg itself meets criteria; the pulse increase of 22 bpm supports volume depletion.
Supine and standing readings are sufficient; a sitting reading is optional and used when the client cannot stand safely.
Correct. A drop of ≥20 mm Hg systolic or ≥10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing is orthostatic hypotension; the diuretic and compensatory tachycardia suggest volume depletion.
questions.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is SBP ↓ ≥20 or DBP ↓ ≥10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing. Diuretics, antihypertensives, dehydration, bleeding, and prolonged bed rest are common causes. The nurse should implement fall precautions and notify the provider.
questions.takeaway: Orthostatic = SBP ↓ ≥20 or DBP ↓ ≥10 within 3 minutes of standing.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Pulse, Peripheral & Cardiovascular Assessment
questions.hintContent: Recall how a pulse deficit is calculated and why some heartbeats may not reach the wrist.
questions.hintStrategy: Calculate first, then choose the option that explains the physiologic meaning of the difference.
questions.stem: Two nurses assess a client with an irregular rhythm simultaneously for 1 minute. The apical rate is 110/min and the radial rate is 92/min. What is the best interpretation of this finding?
options: There is a pulse deficit of 18, meaning some contractions are not perfusing the periphery.
One of the nurses miscounted, because the rates should always be identical.
The client has a 2+ radial pulse and a normal apical rate.
The radial rate is the more accurate value and should be documented alone.
optionRationales: Correct. Pulse deficit = apical − radial (110 − 92 = 18). Some ventricular contractions are too weak to produce a palpable peripheral pulse, as in atrial fibrillation.
The rates are normally identical, but a difference is a real, clinically significant finding in dysrhythmias — not simply an error.
An apical rate of 110 is tachycardic, and the amplitude of a pulse is not described by this data.
The apical rate reflects actual heartbeats; both rates and the deficit should be documented.
questions.rationale: An apical-radial pulse is performed by two nurses counting at the same time for a full minute. A pulse deficit indicates ineffective contractions and reduced cardiac output. The radial rate can never exceed the apical rate.
questions.takeaway: Pulse deficit = apical − radial; it means some beats aren't perfusing.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Pulse, Peripheral & Cardiovascular Assessment
questions.hintContent: Review the 0–4+ pulse amplitude scale and how each grade feels under your fingers.
questions.hintStrategy: Focus on the two descriptors in the stem: 'faint' and 'easily obliterated.'
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse palpates a client's dorsalis pedis pulse and finds it faint and easily obliterated with light pressure. How should the nurse document the amplitude of this pulse?
optionRationales: 0 indicates an absent pulse that cannot be palpated at all.
Correct. A 1+ pulse is diminished, weak, or thready and easily obliterated.
2+ is a normal, easily palpable pulse that is not easily obliterated.
3+ is a full, increased pulse.
questions.rationale: Pulse amplitude is graded 0 (absent), 1+ (diminished/weak), 2+ (normal), 3+ (full/increased), and 4+ (bounding). Compare bilaterally and use a Doppler when a pulse cannot be palpated.
questions.takeaway: Weak and easily obliterated = 1+.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Pulse, Peripheral & Cardiovascular Assessment
questions.hintContent: Recall what distended neck veins reflect about right atrial/central venous pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: Cluster the cues (neck veins + ankle edema) and ask which side of the circulation is backed up.
questions.stem: With the head of the bed at 45°, the nurse observes the client's internal jugular vein pulsation 7 cm above the sternal angle. The client has 2+ pitting edema of both ankles. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?
options: Hypovolemia from inadequate oral intake
Peripheral arterial disease
Right-sided heart failure with fluid overload
Orthostatic hypotension
optionRationales: Hypovolemia causes flat neck veins, not distention.
PAD affects arterial flow (weak pulses, pallor, claudication) and does not cause JVD.
Correct. JVD more than 3–4 cm above the sternal angle at 30–45° reflects elevated right atrial pressure; with dependent edema this suggests right-sided HF/fluid overload.
Orthostatic hypotension is a BP change with position and is associated with low volume, not JVD.
questions.rationale: Jugular veins normally appear flat when the client sits at 45°. Distention indicates increased central venous pressure, as seen with right-sided HF, fluid overload, or cardiac tamponade.
questions.takeaway: JVD + dependent edema = right-sided backup (right HF/fluid overload).

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Hemostasis & Fibrinolysis
questions.hintContent: Recall the final step of hemostasis — how the body normally removes a clot once healing occurs.
questions.hintStrategy: Distinguish drugs that PREVENT clots from drugs that DISSOLVE clots; the daughter is asking how this drug restores flow.
questions.stem: A client with an acute ischemic stroke is receiving IV alteplase. The client's daughter asks the nurse, 'How is this medicine supposed to help my mom?' Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: It keeps platelets from sticking together so a new clot cannot form.
It blocks vitamin K so the liver makes fewer clotting factors.
It thins the blood so it can flow around the clot more easily.
It activates the body's own clot-dissolving enzyme, which breaks down the clot.
optionRationales: This describes an antiplatelet agent such as aspirin or clopidogrel, which prevents new clots but does not dissolve an existing one.
This describes warfarin, which reduces production of vitamin K–dependent factors over several days.
Anticoagulants are often called 'blood thinners,' but they prevent clot growth; they do not restore flow through an occluded artery.
Correct. Alteplase is manufactured tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). It converts plasminogen to plasmin, which digests the fibrin holding the clot together and restores blood flow.
questions.rationale: Normal fibrinolysis begins when healing tissue releases tPA, which converts plasminogen to plasmin; plasmin digests fibrin and dissolves the clot. Thrombolytics such as alteplase and tenecteplase use this pathway. Because they dissolve clots anywhere in the body, the major risk is bleeding — especially intracranial hemorrhage — so the nurse monitors neurologic status and BP closely.
questions.takeaway: Thrombolytics (tPA) dissolve the clot via plasmin; anticoagulants and antiplatelets only prevent new clotting.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Hemostasis & VTE Prevention
questions.hintContent: Recall the contraindications to mechanical compression and the danger of compressing a limb containing a clot.
questions.hintStrategy: You are looking for the client in whom the ordered device could cause harm. Look for new cues that suggest a complication.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing clients who have prescriptions for sequential compression devices (SCDs). For which client should the nurse withhold the SCD and contact the provider?
options: A client on day 2 after hip replacement whose left calf is newly swollen, warm, and tender
A client on bed rest after a stroke who has intact skin and 2+ pedal pulses
A client receiving subcutaneous enoxaparin after abdominal surgery
A client who reports the sleeves feel warm and makes the legs sweat
optionRationales: Correct. Unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and tenderness suggest DVT. Compression could dislodge the clot and cause a pulmonary embolism; hold the device and notify the provider.
This client is an appropriate candidate for SCDs, which reduce venous stasis during immobility.
Mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis are often used together after surgery.
Warmth and sweating are comfort issues managed with skin care; they are not contraindications.
questions.rationale: SCDs prevent venous stasis, but they are contraindicated in a limb with known or suspected DVT, severe PAD, dermatitis, open wounds, or a recent skin graft. The RN assesses legs before application.
questions.takeaway: Suspected DVT in the limb → no SCD; notify the provider.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Diagnostic Tests
questions.hintContent: Recall how many hours after myocardial injury troponin becomes detectable.
questions.hintStrategy: Note the timing in the stem (1 hour after onset). Be wary of any option that offers false reassurance.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client arrives in the emergency department 1 hour after the onset of substernal chest pressure. The initial troponin level is within normal limits. The client asks, 'Does this mean I didn't have a heart attack?' Which response by the nurse is best?
options: Yes. A normal troponin rules out a heart attack, so you can go home soon.
Troponin can take a few hours to rise, so the test will be repeated to be sure.
Troponin only measures muscle damage in your legs, so we will check a different test.
Your ECG is more reliable than blood tests, so the troponin is not important.
optionRationales: A single early troponin cannot rule out MI; discharging on this basis would be unsafe.
Correct. Troponin rises about 3–4 hours after injury (high-sensitivity assays within 1–3 hours), so serial levels are drawn.
Troponin I and T are cardiac-specific markers, not skeletal muscle markers.
ECG and troponin are complementary; many MIs (NSTEMI) have no diagnostic ECG changes and are diagnosed by troponin.
questions.rationale: Troponin is the most specific biomarker of myocardial injury but takes time to become detectable. Protocols use serial measurements (e.g., at 0 and 1–3 hours) with ECGs and symptom evaluation.
questions.takeaway: One early normal troponin never rules out MI — trend it.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Diagnostic Tests · Cardiac Catheterization
questions.hintContent: Recall that the femoral puncture is arterial and how quickly arterial bleeding can cause shock.
questions.hintStrategy: The stem asks what to do FIRST. Choose the action that directly stops the threat rather than one that only gathers data or delegates.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Two hours after a cardiac catheterization via the right femoral artery, the client says, 'My groin suddenly feels warm and wet.' Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Check the right pedal pulses and compare them with the left
Take a full set of vital signs
Apply firm direct pressure just above the puncture site
Notify the interventional cardiologist
optionRationales: Pulse checks are important but come after controlling arterial bleeding.
Vital signs are needed but should not delay stopping the bleeding.
Correct. A warm, wet sensation suggests arterial bleeding. Direct manual pressure proximal to the skin puncture (over the arterial puncture) controls hemorrhage immediately.
The provider must be notified, but the nurse should first stop the bleeding and call for help while maintaining pressure.
questions.rationale: Femoral arterial bleeding can quickly cause hypovolemic shock. The first priority is to control the hemorrhage with direct pressure while summoning help, then assess vital signs and distal pulses and notify the provider.
questions.takeaway: Bleeding at a femoral site → pressure first, then call and assess.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Diagnostic Tests · Cardiac Catheterization
questions.hintContent: Recall how iodinated contrast affects the kidneys and why metformin is a concern with renal impairment.
questions.hintStrategy: Scan each option for a value outside normal limits; the one that increases procedural risk is what you report.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the data of a client scheduled for cardiac catheterization with contrast in 2 hours. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider before the procedure?
options: Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL
Potassium 4.2 mEq/L
Client has been NPO except sips of water with morning medications
Serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL in a client taking metformin
optionRationales: This hemoglobin is within normal limits.
This potassium is within normal limits.
Taking morning medications with sips of water is generally acceptable unless the protocol says otherwise.

Correct. Iodinated contrast is nephrotoxic. An elevated creatinine indicates impaired renal function, raising the risk of contrast-induced kidney injury, and metformin with renal impairment increases the risk of lactic acidosis.
questions.rationale: Before cardiac catheterization the nurse checks renal function, coagulation studies, allergies, anticoagulants, and metformin use. Abnormal kidney function may require hydration protocols, holding metformin, or reconsidering contrast volume.
questions.takeaway: Contrast + high creatinine (especially with metformin) → report before the procedure.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Case Study B.E. Part 1 · Stroke Recognition
questions.hintContent: Recall which treatment decisions in acute ischemic stroke depend on timing.
questions.hintStrategy: Several options are true health information. Choose the one that changes immediate emergency treatment.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: B.E., a 64-year-old man with CAD, hypertension, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and diabetes, arrives in the emergency department after collapsing at home. His wife reports that before he lost consciousness he was confused, had left-arm numbness and double vision, slurred speech, and left facial droop. He is now awake. Which information is most important for the nurse to obtain from the wife immediately?
options: The exact time he was last seen normal
Whether he has had a recent influenza vaccine
The name of his cardiologist
Whether he follows a low-sodium diet
optionRationales: Correct. Time last known well determines eligibility for IV thrombolysis (within 4.5 hours) and thrombectomy; every minute of delay costs neurons.
Vaccination status is not relevant to acute stroke decision-making.
The cardiologist's name can be obtained later; it does not affect immediate treatment.
Dietary adherence is a health promotion issue, not an emergency priority.
questions.rationale: B.E. has classic BE-FAST findings. Stroke treatment is time-dependent, so establishing when he was last known well is essential, along with activating the stroke team, checking glucose, and obtaining a stat noncontrast CT.
questions.takeaway: Suspected stroke: 'When was he last known well?' is the first question.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Case Study B.E. Part 1 · Acute Stroke Care
questions.hintContent: Recall the major complication associated with facial droop and slurred speech after stroke and what must happen before oral intake.
questions.hintStrategy: Consider whether any form of oral intake is safe yet; watch for options that only modify how the liquid is given.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: B.E., 64, is being evaluated for an acute stroke; he has slurred speech and left facial droop. He tells the nurse he is very thirsty and asks for a cup of water. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Provide water through a straw so he can control the amount
Offer ice chips instead of water
Explain that he cannot have anything by mouth until his swallowing has been screened
Provide thickened water and have him sit upright
optionRationales: Straws increase the risk of aspiration in a client with possible dysphagia.
Ice chips are still oral intake and pose an aspiration risk before a swallow screen.
Correct. Clients with suspected stroke remain NPO (including medications) until a bedside dysphagia screen is passed — a Class 1 recommendation — because aspiration pneumonia is a major complication.
Thickened liquids are ordered after a swallow evaluation; they are not given before screening.
questions.rationale: Facial droop and slurred speech signal possible dysphagia. Aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of complications after stroke, so the nurse keeps the client NPO and provides mouth care until swallowing is screened.
questions.takeaway: Stroke → NPO until a swallow screen is passed.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Case Study B.E. Part 2 · Fluid Overload
questions.hintContent: Recall the ABC priority framework and how positioning affects venous return and lung expansion.
questions.hintStrategy: The stem asks what to do FIRST while help is on the way. Which option addresses airway and breathing right now?
questions.stem: B.E., 64, is in the ICU 36 hours after an ischemic stroke. He has bilateral crackles (worse on the right), pooled oral secretions, SpO₂ 87% on a nonrebreather mask, RR 30, pitting edema of the legs, and decreased urine output. He is difficult to arouse. The provider and respiratory therapist have been called. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to measure output accurately
Raise the head of the bed and suction the oropharynx
Obtain a daily weight using a bed scale
Draw a serum BNP level
optionRationales: Accurate output measurement is needed, but it does not address the immediate airway and oxygenation threat.
Correct. Airway and breathing come first: raising the HOB reduces venous return and improves lung expansion, and suctioning clears secretions he cannot manage, reducing aspiration.
Weight helps track fluid status but is not an emergency action.
BNP supports a diagnosis of heart failure but does not treat hypoxemia.
questions.rationale: B.E. shows fluid overload/pulmonary edema and possible aspiration (right-sided crackles; the right mainstem bronchus is straighter). With hypoxemia and decreased LOC, airway and breathing are the priority until the provider and RT arrive to evaluate the need for mechanical ventilation.
questions.takeaway: Hypoxemic client with secretions → position upright and clear the airway first.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Case Study B.E. Part 3 · Hypertensive Emergency
questions.hintContent: Recall the recommended rate of BP reduction in a hypertensive emergency and why a recent stroke makes rapid lowering dangerous.
questions.hintStrategy: Beware of options that sound aggressive or complete. The goal in the first hour is controlled, partial reduction.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: B.E., 64, is on day 4 after an ischemic stroke and is mechanically ventilated. His BP is 258/128 (confirmed on repeat), P 112, and pink frothy secretions are being suctioned. The provider prescribes a nicardipine infusion. Which BP goal should the nurse anticipate for the first hour of therapy?
options: Normalize the BP to less than 120/80 within 30 minutes
Lower the SBP below 140 within 15 minutes to protect the brain
Reduce the BP by no more than about 25% within the first hour
Avoid lowering the BP until the pulmonary edema resolves
optionRationales: Rapid normalization can cause cerebral, coronary, and renal ischemia — especially dangerous in a client with a recent stroke.
An abrupt drop of this size risks extending the stroke by reducing cerebral perfusion.
Correct. In hypertensive emergency, BP is lowered in a controlled way — generally no more than 25% in the first hour, then to about 160/100–110 over the next 2–6 hours.
Severe hypertension is increasing afterload and driving the pulmonary edema; it must be treated promptly.
questions.rationale: B.E. has severe hypertension with acute target-organ damage (pulmonary edema) — a hypertensive emergency. Titratable IV agents in the ICU allow gradual, controlled lowering. The nurse also assesses and treats contributing factors such as pain and agitation (he grimaced during the sedation vacation).
questions.takeaway: Hypertensive emergency: lower BP ≤25% in the first hour — controlled, not crashed.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Lifespan Considerations · Pregnancy
questions.hintContent: Recall what the gravid uterus compresses when a client lies flat in late pregnancy.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the cause of the hypotension first; the best first action removes the cause quickly and noninvasively.
questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks' gestation lying flat for an ultrasound reports feeling dizzy and nauseated. She is pale and clammy, and her BP is 88/50 (baseline 114/70). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Place the client in Trendelenburg position
Increase the IV fluid rate
Administer oxygen at 10 L/min by nonrebreather mask
Turn the client to her left side
optionRationales: Trendelenburg does not relieve compression of the vena cava and increases pressure on the diaphragm.
The cause is mechanical compression, not volume loss; fluids are not the first action.
Oxygen may be used later but does not correct the cause.
Correct. Supine hypotensive syndrome results from the gravid uterus compressing the inferior vena cava. Left lateral positioning (or a wedge under the right hip) restores venous return.
questions.rationale: When a pregnant client lies supine, the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava, reducing venous return to the right atrium, cardiac output, and BP. Repositioning is fast and corrects the problem.
questions.takeaway: Supine, dizzy, hypotensive pregnant client → turn to the left side.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Lifespan Considerations · Infants and Children
questions.hintContent: Recall which pulse site is most accurate in infants and how long to count.
questions.hintStrategy: Two variables are being tested in each option: the technique AND the timing relative to the injections.
questions.stem: The nurse is obtaining vital signs on a 4-month-old infant before immunizations. Which technique for assessing the pulse is most appropriate?
options: Auscultate the apical pulse for 1 full minute before giving the injections
Palpate the radial pulse for 30 seconds and multiply by 2
Palpate the carotid pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4
Auscultate the apical pulse for 30 seconds after giving the injections
optionRationales: Correct. The apical pulse is used for infants and young children, counted for a full minute because infant rates are irregular, and taken before painful procedures that would raise the rate.
The radial pulse is difficult to palpate accurately in infants.
The carotid is not used for routine infant pulse assessment, and 15-second counts are inaccurate for infants.
Assessing after injections gives an artificially high rate from crying and pain.
questions.rationale: For infants and children up to about 2–3 years, the apical pulse is the most accurate. Counting for a full minute accounts for sinus arrhythmia, and assessing before uncomfortable procedures prevents falsely elevated values.
questions.takeaway: Infants: apical pulse, full minute, before anything that makes them cry.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Lifespan Considerations · Older Adults
questions.hintContent: Recall how cardiac problems often present in older adults and whether the absence of chest pain rules out MI.
questions.hintStrategy: Before treating a behavior, look for the physiologic cause. Choose the option that assesses rather than labels.
questions.stem: An 82-year-old client with a history of hypertension and coronary artery disease had 2 falls this week and is newly confused and agitated. The client denies chest pain. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply a bed alarm and document the falls in an incident report
Assess the apical pulse, BP (including orthostatic readings), and oxygen saturation
Reorient the client frequently and request a psychiatric consultation
Explain to the family that confusion is an expected part of aging
optionRationales: Safety measures are important but do not identify the cause of the new change.
Correct. In older adults, falls, confusion, and agitation may be the first signs of a cardiac problem (MI, dysrhythmia, HF, or orthostatic hypotension). Assessing perfusion comes first.
Reorientation is supportive, but a physiologic cause must be ruled out before attributing the change to a psychiatric condition.
New confusion is never a normal part of aging and must be investigated.
questions.rationale: Older adults often present atypically; the absence of chest pain does not exclude MI. The nurse assesses cardiovascular status to identify decreased perfusion or dysrhythmia before addressing the behavior itself.
questions.takeaway: New falls or confusion in an older adult → assess perfusion first; it may be the heart.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Health Promotion
questions.hintContent: Recall the BMI ranges for normal weight, overweight, and obese.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a negatively worded item: you are looking for the INCORRECT statement by the client.
questions.stem: The nurse has taught a client with stage 1 hypertension and an LDL of 162 mg/dL about reducing cardiovascular risk. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: I'll aim for at least 150 minutes of brisk walking each week.
I'm going to read food labels and cut back on sodium.
My goal is to keep my body mass index below 30.
I'll limit myself to no more than one alcoholic drink a day.
optionRationales: This meets the recommendation for moderate aerobic activity.
Reducing sodium is an effective lifestyle measure for lowering BP.
Correct — needs further teaching. A BMI of 25–29.9 is overweight; the heart-healthy goal is a BMI below 25.
Limiting alcohol (≤1 drink/day for women, ≤2 for men) is consistent with recommendations.
questions.rationale: Modifiable risk factors include smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, inactivity, poor diet, excess alcohol, and stress. A BMI under 25 is the target; a goal of under 30 would still allow the client to be overweight.
questions.takeaway: Heart-healthy BMI goal is <25, not <30.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Stroke Recognition (BE-FAST)
questions.hintContent: Recall the letters of BE-FAST and the importance of SUDDEN onset.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option for two cues: is it neurologic, and is it sudden? Chronic or systemic complaints point elsewhere.
questions.stem: A telehealth nurse receives a call from a woman about her 70-year-old husband, who has atrial fibrillation. Which findings she describes should prompt the nurse to instruct her to call 911 immediately for a possible stroke? Select all that apply.
options: He suddenly started stumbling and can't keep his balance.
He says he is seeing double since lunch.
The right side of his mouth is drooping.
His calves cramp when he walks and ease when he rests, as they have for months.
His words are coming out slurred and jumbled.
He has had a low-grade fever and chills since yesterday.
optionRationales: Correct. B = Balance.
Correct. E = Eyes.
Correct. F = Face drooping.
Chronic, activity-related calf cramping relieved by rest is intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease — not a sudden neurologic change.
Correct. S = Speech difficulty.
Fever and chills suggest infection, not a stroke warning sign.
questions.rationale: BE-FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time. The key cue is sudden onset, and atrial fibrillation raises the risk of embolic stroke. The nurse directs the caller to activate EMS rather than drive him in, and to note when he was last known well.
questions.takeaway: BE-FAST — sudden onset; call 911 and note the time.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure Assessment
questions.hintContent: Recall the preparation, positioning, cuff placement, and deflation rate for accurate BP measurement.
questions.hintStrategy: For each action, ask whether it would make the reading falsely high, falsely low, or accurate.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is observing a new graduate measure a client's blood pressure manually. Which actions indicate correct technique? Select all that apply.
options: Has the client sit quietly for 5 minutes with back supported and feet flat on the floor
Supports the client's arm so the cuff is at heart level
Places the cuff over the client's thin shirt sleeve
Deflates the cuff at 2–3 mm Hg per second
Reinflates the cuff immediately on the same arm to confirm a reading
Chats with the client during the reading to help the client relax
optionRationales: Correct. Rest with back and feet supported reduces falsely elevated readings.
Correct. An arm below heart level falsely raises BP; above heart level falsely lowers it.
The cuff should be placed on bare skin; clothing interferes with accuracy.
Correct. This deflation rate allows accurate identification of Korotkoff sounds.
Wait 1–2 minutes before repeating on the same arm to allow venous congestion to resolve.
Talking during the measurement can raise BP; the client and nurse should not talk.
questions.rationale: Accurate BP requires a rested client, correct cuff size on a bare arm, arm supported at heart level, no talking, slow deflation, and adequate time between readings. Small errors can misclassify a client's hypertension stage.
questions.takeaway: Rest 5 min, bare arm at heart level, no talking, deflate 2–3 mm Hg/s.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Failure
questions.hintContent: Recall where blood backs up when the left ventricle fails versus when the right ventricle fails.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding by the organ system it affects: lungs versus systemic veins/abdomen.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with acute left-sided heart failure. Which assessment findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Crackles in the lung bases
Needing 3 pillows to sleep
Pink, frothy sputum
Hepatomegaly and ascites
Jugular venous distention at 45°
Dyspnea when walking to the bathroom
optionRationales: Correct. Blood backs up into the pulmonary circulation, causing crackles.
Correct. Orthopnea results from pulmonary congestion that worsens when lying flat.
Correct. Pink, frothy sputum indicates pulmonary edema from severe left-sided failure.
Hepatomegaly and ascites result from systemic venous congestion — right-sided HF.
JVD reflects elevated right-sided pressures — right-sided HF.
Correct. Exertional dyspnea reflects pulmonary congestion and reduced cardiac output.
questions.rationale: Left-sided HF backs up into the lungs (dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, cough, pink frothy sputum). Right-sided HF backs up into the systemic veins (JVD, edema, hepatomegaly, ascites). Left-sided failure frequently progresses to right-sided failure.
questions.takeaway: Left = Lungs; Right = Rest of the body.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Acute Pulmonary Edema
questions.hintContent: Recall how preload contributes to pulmonary edema and which interventions reduce it.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask: does this add volume/venous return to the lungs, or remove it?
questions.stem: A client with heart failure suddenly develops severe dyspnea, crackles throughout both lung fields, pink frothy sputum, and SpO₂ of 84%. Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Position in high Fowler's with legs dependent
Administer high-flow oxygen and prepare for noninvasive ventilation
Administer IV furosemide as prescribed
Maintain strict intake and output
Place in Trendelenburg position to support BP
Administer a 500 mL normal saline bolus
optionRationales: Correct. Sitting upright with legs down reduces venous return (preload) and eases breathing.
Correct. Oxygenation is the immediate priority; NIPPV reduces preload and improves gas exchange.
Correct. A loop diuretic removes excess fluid and provides venodilation.
Correct. Accurate I&O evaluates diuretic response and fluid balance.
Head-down positioning increases venous return and worsens pulmonary congestion.
A fluid bolus adds volume and would worsen pulmonary edema.
questions.rationale: Acute pulmonary edema is a medical emergency caused by elevated LV pressures that force fluid into the alveoli. Treatment reduces preload and afterload and supports oxygenation: upright positioning, oxygen/ventilatory support, diuretics, vasodilators, and close monitoring.
questions.takeaway: Pulmonary edema: sit up, legs down, O₂, diurese — never add fluid.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · VTE Prevention · Compression Devices
questions.hintContent: Recall correct sizing and fit for compression devices and the contraindications to their use.
questions.hintStrategy: Some options sound convenient but create a tourniquet or ignore a new cue. Evaluate each for safety.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is applying sequential compression devices and graduated compression stockings to a postoperative client. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Measure the client's legs to select the correct size
Check that two fingers fit between the SCD sleeve and the leg
Remove the devices periodically to inspect the skin per policy
Roll the top of the stocking down if it is too long
Continue compression even if the client develops unilateral calf pain and warmth
optionRationales: Correct. Proper sizing ensures effective compression and prevents skin injury.
Correct. A two-finger fit confirms the sleeve is snug but not constrictive.
Correct. Skin inspection detects pressure injury and allows neurovascular assessment.
Rolling a stocking creates a tight band that acts like a tourniquet and impairs circulation.
Unilateral calf pain and warmth suggest DVT; compression should be stopped on that leg and the provider notified.
questions.rationale: Mechanical prophylaxis reduces venous stasis. The nurse ensures correct fit, smooth application, and regular skin and neurovascular checks, and withholds compression from a limb with suspected DVT or severe arterial disease.
questions.takeaway: Right size, two-finger fit, no rolling, check the skin — and no compression over a suspected clot.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Diagnostic Tests · Cardiac Catheterization
questions.hintContent: Recall the purpose of bed rest and limited hip flexion after femoral arterial access, and how contrast affects the kidneys.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it protects the arterial puncture site and distal perfusion.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client returns to the unit after a left heart catheterization through the right femoral artery, with manual compression used for hemostasis. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess right pedal pulses, color, temperature, and sensation per protocol
Keep the right leg straight during prescribed bed rest
Keep the head of the bed at or below 30°
Encourage oral fluids unless contraindicated
Help the client sit up at 90° to eat lunch
Ambulate the client to the bathroom 30 minutes after arrival
optionRationales: Correct. Neurovascular checks detect arterial occlusion or compromise distal to the puncture.
Correct. Hip flexion can disrupt the clot at the arterial puncture and cause bleeding.
Correct. Limiting head elevation prevents hip flexion at the access site.
Correct. Fluids help flush the nephrotoxic contrast through the kidneys.
Sitting at 90° flexes the hip and increases the risk of bleeding and hematoma.
After manual compression, bed rest typically lasts several hours; early ambulation risks bleeding.
questions.rationale: After femoral access, nursing care focuses on preventing and detecting bleeding, hematoma, retroperitoneal bleeding, and limb ischemia, and protecting the kidneys from contrast injury.
questions.takeaway: Femoral cath: leg straight, HOB ≤30°, frequent pulse checks, push fluids.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure Assessment
questions.hintContent: Review the conditions that make a limb unsafe for BP cuff inflation.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each client separately; ask whether cuff compression could damage a structure or skew the reading in that arm.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The charge nurse is reviewing the plan for vital signs on a medical unit. For which clients should the nurse instruct the UAP not to use the left arm for blood pressure measurement? Select all that apply.
options: A client receiving hemodialysis with an arteriovenous fistula in the left forearm
A client with 0.9% sodium chloride infusing through a left forearm IV
A client who had a left mastectomy with axillary lymph node removal
A client with a fiberglass cast on the left wrist after a fracture
A client with a large, healed tattoo on the left upper arm
optionRationales: Correct. Compression can damage the fistula and cause clotting and loss of dialysis access.
Correct. Cuff inflation interrupts the infusion and can damage the vein.
Correct. Compression increases the risk of lymphedema on the side of node removal.
Correct. A cast prevents cuff placement and the limb may be injured.
A healed tattoo does not affect BP measurement.
questions.rationale: Avoid BP measurement on a limb with an IV infusion, AV fistula/graft, lymph node removal, cast or bulky dressing, or injury/disease. Use the other arm or the thigh.
questions.takeaway: No BP cuff on an arm with an IV, fistula, node dissection, or cast.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Risk Factors
questions.hintContent: Recall the difference between modifiable and nonmodifiable cardiovascular risk factors.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask: could this client change it through behavior or treatment?
questions.stem: A 55-year-old client asks which of their cardiovascular risk factors they can change. Which factors should the nurse identify as modifiable? Select all that apply.
options: Cigarette smoking
Father had an MI at age 48
Elevated LDL cholesterol
Sedentary lifestyle
Age over 50
Blood pressure of 142/90
optionRationales: Correct. Smoking cessation reduces risk.
Family history of early CAD is nonmodifiable.
Correct. Diet, exercise, and statins can lower LDL.
Correct. Increasing physical activity reduces risk.
Age is nonmodifiable.
Correct. Hypertension can be controlled with lifestyle changes and medications.
questions.rationale: Nonmodifiable risk factors include age, sex, race, and family/personal history. Modifiable factors include smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes control, obesity, inactivity, diet, alcohol, and stress.
questions.takeaway: You can't change your genes or your age — but you can change smoking, BP, lipids, and activity.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Lifespan Considerations · Older Adults
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal cardiovascular and pulmonary changes of aging and which blood gas change always indicates pathology.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate expected age-related changes from findings that signal disease — 'common' is not always 'normal.'
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing an 80-year-old client. Which findings are consistent with normal age-related cardiovascular and pulmonary changes? Select all that apply.
options: Isolated systolic blood pressure of 148 mm Hg with a diastolic of 76 mm Hg
Slight decrease in arterial PaO₂
Increased anteroposterior chest diameter
PaCO₂ of 52 mm Hg
New fatigue that limits daily activities
optionRationales: Correct. Arterial stiffening commonly produces isolated systolic hypertension in older adults (though it still warrants treatment).
Correct. Arterial oxygen tension declines modestly with age.
Correct. Changes in chest wall compliance increase AP diameter and residual volume.
An elevated PaCO₂ indicates pathology (hypoventilation), not normal aging.
Fatigue, decreased activity, and sleep disturbance are not normal aging and may signal cardiac disease.
questions.rationale: Aging causes arterial stiffening, valve stiffening, AV node fibrosis, a slight decline in cardiac output, and reduced pulmonary compliance with lower PaO₂. However, elevated PaCO₂ and new fatigue or functional decline are abnormal and warrant investigation.
questions.takeaway: Lower PaO₂ can be aging; high PaCO₂ and new fatigue are not.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Hypertensive Crisis
questions.hintContent: Recall what distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from severe hypertension without acute organ damage.
questions.hintStrategy: The BP is the same in both conditions. Select only findings that show acute damage to a target organ.
questions.stem: A client with a history of nonadherence to antihypertensive medications has a BP of 214/126 mm Hg. Which additional findings indicate that this is a hypertensive emergency rather than severe hypertension without organ damage? Select all that apply.
options: Severe headache with new confusion
Crushing substernal chest pain
Crackles with pink frothy sputum
Serum creatinine that rose from 1.0 to 2.4 mg/dL
Anxiety about being admitted
Reports running out of medications 1 week ago
optionRationales: Correct. Suggests hypertensive encephalopathy or stroke — neurologic target-organ damage.
Correct. Suggests acute coronary syndrome or aortic dissection — cardiovascular target-organ damage.
Correct. Acute pulmonary edema from severe afterload — cardiac target-organ damage.
Correct. Acute kidney injury — renal target-organ damage.
Anxiety is common and may raise BP but does not indicate organ damage.
Nonadherence explains the cause but does not indicate target-organ damage.
questions.rationale: Both severe hypertension and hypertensive emergency involve BP >180/120. What makes it an emergency is acute target-organ damage — brain, heart, lungs, kidneys, eyes, or aorta — which requires ICU admission and titratable IV medications.
questions.takeaway: The number alone doesn't make an emergency — organ damage does.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Cardiac Anatomy & Circulation
questions.hintContent: Recall the path of venous blood from the lower extremities back to the heart and on to the lungs.
questions.hintStrategy: Start at the location of the clot and trace forward with the direction of blood flow.
questions.stem: A client on bed rest has a deep vein thrombosis in the left femoral vein. The client asks how a clot in the leg could end up in the lungs. Place the structures in the order a dislodged clot would travel through them before lodging in the lungs.
options: Iliac vein
Inferior vena cava
Right atrium
Right ventricle
Pulmonary artery
questions.rationale: Venous blood from the leg flows through the femoral and iliac veins into the inferior vena cava, then into the right atrium, through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and through the pulmonic valve into the pulmonary artery. The pulmonary arteries branch into progressively smaller vessels, where the embolus lodges — a pulmonary embolism. Venous clots do not normally reach the left heart or brain because the lungs filter them.
questions.takeaway: Venous clot path: leg vein → IVC → RA → RV → pulmonary artery → PE.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Orthostatic Vital Signs
questions.hintContent: Recall the positions, timing, and criteria used for orthostatic vital signs.
questions.hintStrategy: You need a baseline before a comparison — establish the resting value first.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing orthostatic vital signs for a client who reports dizziness. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Have the client lie supine for about 5 minutes
Measure the BP and pulse while the client is supine
Assist the client to stand, remaining at the bedside
Measure the BP and pulse after 1 and 3 minutes of standing
Compare the readings with orthostatic criteria and document symptoms
questions.rationale: Orthostatic vital signs start with a stable supine baseline, then the client is assisted to stand (or sit if unable to stand safely) and readings are repeated at 1 and 3 minutes. A drop of ≥20 mm Hg SBP or ≥10 mm Hg DBP is positive. The nurse stays with the client to prevent falls.
questions.takeaway: Supine rest → supine VS → stand with help → VS at 1 and 3 min → interpret.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Conduction System & Action Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal conduction pathway and the intrinsic rates of backup pacemakers.
questions.hintStrategy: Begin at the new pacemaker site named in the stem, not at the SA node, and trace the impulse to the ventricles.
questions.stem: A client's SA node has stopped firing, and the monitor now shows a regular junctional rhythm at 48/min originating near the AV node. The nurse explains why the client still has a pulse. Place the structures in the order that an impulse from this new pacemaker site travels to produce ventricular contraction.
options: Atrioventricular (AV) junction
Bundle of His
Right and left bundle branches
Purkinje fibers
questions.rationale: The normal pathway is SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers. When the SA node fails, the AV junction can take over at its intrinsic rate of 40–60/min. The impulse still travels down the normal ventricular pathway, so the QRS is narrow and the ventricles contract — but the slower rate may reduce cardiac output.
questions.takeaway: Backup pacemakers: AV junction 40–60, ventricles 20–40 — the impulse still flows His → bundle branches → Purkinje.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Apical-Radial Pulse
questions.hintContent: Recall how an apical-radial pulse is performed and how the pulse deficit is calculated.
questions.hintStrategy: Think preparation → location → coordination → counting → calculation.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Two nurses are obtaining an apical-radial pulse on a client with atrial fibrillation. Place the steps in the order the nurses should perform them.
options: Perform hand hygiene and explain the procedure to the client
Locate the apical pulse at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line, and the radial pulse
Agree to use one watch and a single signal to start counting
Count the apical and radial rates simultaneously for 60 seconds
Subtract the radial rate from the apical rate and document the pulse deficit
questions.rationale: Accurate apical-radial measurement requires two nurses counting at the same time for a full minute with one timepiece. The difference between the rates is the pulse deficit, which reflects contractions that are not perfusing the periphery.
questions.takeaway: Same watch, same start, full minute, apical minus radial.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Failure
questions.hintContent: Recall where fluid accumulates when each ventricle fails.
questions.hintStrategy: For each finding, ask whether it involves the lungs or the systemic venous circulation.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing assessment findings for clients with heart failure. For each finding, indicate whether it is more characteristic of left-sided or right-sided heart failure.
optionRationales: Left-sided: pulmonary congestion worsens when lying flat.
Right-sided: elevated right atrial pressure distends the neck veins.
Left-sided: blood backs up into the pulmonary circulation.
Right-sided: systemic venous congestion engorges the liver and causes ascites.
Right-sided: systemic venous congestion causes fluid to collect in dependent areas.
questions.rationale: Left-sided HF impairs forward flow into the aorta and backs blood into the lungs. Right-sided HF backs blood into the systemic veins. Clients often have both, since left-sided failure is the most common cause of right-sided failure.
questions.takeaway: Left = lungs; Right = rest of the body.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Case Study B.E. Part 2 · Fluid Overload
questions.hintContent: Recall why urine output falls in heart failure and how dysphagia affects oral intake after stroke.
questions.hintStrategy: Interpret the low urine output in context (crackles, edema) before deciding whether fluids help or harm.
questions.stem: B.E., 64, is 36 hours post ischemic stroke with a history of heart failure. He now has bilateral crackles, pitting edema of the legs, decreased urine output, and difficulty managing secretions. For each intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated at this time.
rows: Obtain daily weights on the same scale at the same time
Elevate the head of the bed at least 30°
Administer a 1,000 mL normal saline bolus for low urine output
Offer thin oral liquids to prevent dehydration
optionRationales: Indicated. Daily weight is the most reliable indicator of fluid gain or loss.
Indicated. Accurate I&O tracks fluid balance and the response to diuretics.
Indicated. Elevation reduces aspiration risk and venous return and improves ventilation.
Not indicated. Low urine output here reflects poor cardiac output and fluid overload; a fluid bolus would worsen pulmonary edema.
Not indicated. He has dysphagia and cannot manage secretions; thin liquids create a high aspiration risk.
questions.rationale: B.E.'s low urine output is from decreased cardiac output with fluid overload, not dehydration. Care focuses on monitoring fluid status, protecting the airway, and supporting oxygenation while the team considers diuretics and mechanical ventilation.
questions.takeaway: Oliguria plus crackles and edema = overload — don't give fluid; protect the airway.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Lifespan Considerations · Pregnancy
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal hematologic and hemodynamic changes of pregnancy, including when BP is lowest.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate physiologic adaptations of pregnancy from findings that suggest a complication.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for a client at 32 weeks' gestation. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or unexpected during pregnancy.
rows: Resting pulse 12 bpm higher than prepregnancy baseline
BP of 150/98 mm Hg on two readings
WBC count of 13,000/mm³ with no signs of infection
Swelling, warmth, and pain in the right calf only
optionRationales: Expected. Pulse rises about 10–15 bpm as cardiac output increases.
Expected. Plasma volume expands more than red cell mass, causing physiologic anemia (slight Hct decrease).
Unexpected. BP normally falls in the second trimester and returns toward baseline; ≥140/90 after 20 weeks suggests gestational hypertension or preeclampsia.
Expected. Leukocyte production increases in pregnancy without indicating infection.
Unexpected. Pregnancy is hypercoagulable; unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and pain suggest DVT.
questions.rationale: Pregnancy increases blood volume (40–50%), cardiac output, pulse, WBCs, and clotting factors, and lowers Hct slightly. Hypertension and signs of thrombosis are not normal and require prompt evaluation.
questions.takeaway: Higher HR, lower Hct, and higher WBC are expected; high BP and a swollen calf are not.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Diagnostic Tests · Cardiac Catheterization
questions.hintContent: Recall the complications of femoral catheterization, including bleeding that may not be visible.
questions.hintStrategy: For each finding, ask whether it shows adequate perfusion or a threat to circulation or volume.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client 3 hours after a cardiac catheterization via the left femoral artery. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or requires follow-up.
rows: Small area of ecchymosis at the site that is not enlarging
Left foot cool and pale with capillary refill of 5 seconds
New low back pain with HR 118 and BP 92/58
optionRationales: Expected. Equal, normal pulses indicate adequate distal perfusion.
Expected. Minor bruising is common; mark and monitor for expansion.
Requires follow-up. A cool, pale foot with delayed refill suggests arterial occlusion or thrombus.
Requires follow-up. Back or flank pain with tachycardia and hypotension suggests retroperitoneal bleeding, which may have no visible external signs.
Expected. Adequate urine output suggests good renal perfusion and contrast clearance.
questions.rationale: After femoral catheterization, the nurse monitors for bleeding, hematoma, retroperitoneal hemorrhage, limb ischemia, dysrhythmias, and contrast-induced kidney injury. Changes in distal perfusion or hemodynamics require immediate notification.
questions.takeaway: Back pain + tachycardia + hypotension after femoral cath = retroperitoneal bleed until proven otherwise.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Case Study B.E. Part 1 · Thrombolysis
questions.hintContent: Recall the BP thresholds required before and after IV thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare BOTH the systolic and diastolic values to the threshold before choosing whether it is met.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: B.E., 64, has an acute ischemic stroke confirmed by noncontrast CT, with a last-known-well time 2 hours ago. His BP is 182/98. The team is evaluating him for IV thrombolysis. Complete the statement.
questions.template: Before a thrombolytic can be given, BP must be below {0}. B.E.'s current BP {1} this threshold. After the thrombolytic, the nurse should maintain BP below {2} for 24 hours.

options: meets
exceeds
is irrelevant to

questions.rationale: Current AHA/ASA guidance requires BP <185/110 before starting IV thrombolysis and <180/105 during and for 24 hours after, to reduce the risk of intracranial hemorrhage. At 182/98 (SBP <185 and DBP <110), B.E. meets the BP criterion, although other eligibility factors (such as anticoagulant use for his atrial fibrillation) must also be reviewed. Clients who do not receive thrombolysis are usually allowed permissive hypertension up to 220/120.
questions.takeaway: Thrombolysis BP: <185/110 before, <180/105 after.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Cardiac Output
questions.hintContent: Recall the CO formula, the normal CO range, and what happens to ventricular filling at very fast rates.
questions.hintStrategy: Convert milliliters to liters carefully, then apply the formula conceptually for the second half.
questions.stem: A client at rest has a heart rate of 80/min and a stroke volume of 70 mL. Complete the statement.
questions.template: The client's cardiac output is {0}, which is {1}. If the heart rate rises to 170/min, cardiac output is likely to {2} because {3}.

options: 1.5 L/min
8.8 L/min
0.56 L/min
5.6 L/min
within normal limits
below normal
above normal
double
stay the same
decrease
afterload decreases
diastolic filling time shortens
contractility is lost
preload becomes excessive

questions.rationale: CO = HR × SV = 80 × 70 mL = 5,600 mL/min, or 5.6 L/min, which is within the normal 4–8 L/min range. At very fast rates diastole shortens so much that the ventricles cannot fill, stroke volume falls, and cardiac output drops despite the higher rate.
questions.takeaway: CO = HR × SV — but past ~150 bpm, filling time is lost and CO falls.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Case Study B.E. Part 3 · Hypertensive Emergency
questions.hintContent: Recall the definition of a hypertensive emergency and how pain affects sympathetic tone.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the evidence that proves target-organ damage, not just any abnormal finding.
questions.stem: B.E., 64, is on day 4 after an ischemic stroke and is mechanically ventilated. BP is 258/128, P 112, crackles are heard throughout the lungs, and the nurse is suctioning pink frothy secretions. During a sedation vacation, he is minimally responsive and grimaces as if in pain. Complete the statement.
questions.template: B.E. is most likely experiencing {0}, as evidenced by {1}. A contributing factor the nurse should also assess and treat is {2}.

options: severe hypertension without organ damage
hypovolemic shock
an expected post-stroke BP rise
a hypertensive emergency
a heart rate of 112
minimal responsiveness during sedation vacation
pink frothy secretions and diffuse crackles
hypoglycemia
pain and agitation
hypothermia

questions.rationale: BP >180/120 with acute target-organ damage — here, acute pulmonary edema — defines a hypertensive emergency. Tachycardia and decreased responsiveness are nonspecific. His grimacing suggests pain, which increases sympathetic tone and BP, so pain and sedation needs should be addressed along with titrated IV antihypertensive therapy.
questions.takeaway: Hypertensive emergency = severe BP + acute organ damage; treat pain and agitation too.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Lifespan Considerations · Infants and Children
questions.hintContent: Recall the pediatric SBP estimation formulas and how children respond to severe hypoxemia compared with adults.
questions.hintStrategy: Plug the child's age into the formulas; then consider whether a falling heart rate in a hypoxic child is reassuring or ominous.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 6-year-old child in the pediatric clinic. Complete the statement.
questions.template: Using the common estimate, the child's expected median systolic BP is about {0} mm Hg, and hypotension would be a systolic BP below about {1} mm Hg. If this child became hypoxemic and the heart rate began to fall, the nurse should recognize this as {2}.

options: an expected compensatory response
an ominous sign of impending arrest
a sign of improving oxygenation

questions.rationale: For children aged 1–10, median SBP ≈ 90 + (2 × age) = 102 mm Hg, and the lower limit ≈ 70 + (2 × age) = 82 mm Hg. Children respond to severe hypoxemia with bradycardia, whereas adults become tachycardic; bradycardia in a hypoxemic child signals impending cardiopulmonary arrest.
questions.takeaway: Kids: SBP ≈ 90 + 2×age; hypoxemia + bradycardia = pre-arrest.
